summary_html: Cases arising on **federal lands/facilities** or involving **Indian children** invoke federal/tribal jurisdictional rules (VICAA for federal facilities; **ICWA** for Indian children and tribal preference/jurisdiction).
authority_html:
- **VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — federal-facility reporting mandates  
- **ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901–1963)** — tribal jurisdiction, placement preferences, notice to tribes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Indian Child Welfare Act is within Congress's Article I power and that its requirements do not unconstitutionally commandeer the States, and that the petitioners lacked standing to press the equal protection and nondelegation challenges to the placement preferences.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling federal authority that ICWA validly governs state child custody proceedings involving Indian children, including its notice, active efforts, heightened proof and qualified expert witness requirements.
key_cases.quote: But the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' in ICWA section 1911(a) has a uniform federal meaning under which children take the reservation domicile of their parents, so the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction over twins born and voluntarily surrendered off the reservation and the state adoption decree had to be vacated.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading decision on when the tribal jurisdiction trigger fires: a state court has no jurisdiction over an Indian child domiciled on a reservation, and parents cannot defeat that jurisdiction by placing the child off-reservation.
key_cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

mandatory_reporters: Any person (universal mandatory reporting) — N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 169-C:29
Physicians, surgeons, county medical examiners, psychiatrists, residents, interns
Registered nurses and hospital personnel (admission, examination, care and treatment)
Teachers, school officials, school nurses, school counselors
Social workers, day care workers, and any other child or foster care workers
reporting_details: New Hampshire is a universal-reporter state: RSA 169-C:29 lists physicians, dentists, psychologists, registered nurses and hospital personnel, teachers, school officials and school nurses, social workers, day care and other child or foster care workers, law enforcement officials and clergy, and closes with “any other person having reason to suspect that a child has been abused or neglected,” all of whom “shall report the same in accordance with this chapter.” RSA 169-C:30 sets the route and the form: an oral report “shall be made immediately by telephone or otherwise, and followed within 48 hours by a report in writing, if so requested, to the department” — the Department of Health and Human Services, which takes reports through the DCYF Central Intake Unit at 603-271-6562 or 1-800-894-5533 (in-state only), staffed 24 hours a day including weekends and holidays.
